guides.title: Close Reading & Literary Analysis
guides.summary: Close reading is the disciplined study of a text's language and form to understand how it makes meaning. This guide covers the practice's history, the features of language a reader learns to notice, and how observations become interpretive arguments.

sections.heading: What Close Reading Is
sections.body: Close reading is the disciplined, attentive study of a text's language, its words, images, sounds, rhythms, and structures, in order to understand how the text produces its meaning and its effects. It treats a poem, a passage of prose, or a scene of drama, not as a transparent window through which to glimpse a message that could be paraphrased away, but as a made object whose particular arrangement of words is itself the meaning. To read closely is to slow down, to notice detail that ordinary reading passes over, and to ask at every point not only what a text says but how it says it, and why that manner matters. The practice rests on a conviction that in literature, form and content are inseparable. A poem does not merely convey an idea that could have been stated in any other words; it means what it means through this diction, this metaphor, this line-break, this rhythm. Change the words and you change the meaning. Close reading therefore takes the exact wording seriously, on the assumption that a skilled writer's choices are motivated and that attending to them repays the effort with a richer, more precise understanding than a summary can give. Close reading is both a skill and the foundation of literary analysis. As a skill, it is the habit of careful, curious attention to language that can be applied to anything written. As the basis of analysis, it supplies the concrete evidence, the specific words and features of a text, from which interpretive arguments are built. An essay of literary criticism that is not grounded in close reading tends to float free of the text, asserting themes and meanings without showing how the language supports them; close reading anchors interpretation in what is demonstrably there on the page. It is worth stating what close reading is not. It is not a hunt for hidden symbols that the author secretly planted, nor a game of finding the single correct meaning locked inside the text. It is not the same as summarizing the plot, describing one's feelings, or reporting facts about the author's life. And it does not require esoteric knowledge to begin: its basic tools are attention, patience, and a willingness to ask questions of the words. A close reader looks at what is actually written, notices patterns and tensions, forms hypotheses about how the parts work together, and tests those hypotheses against further detail. The rewards are considerable. Close reading makes one a more perceptive and appreciative reader, alert to craft and nuance that casual reading misses; it disciplines interpretation, tying it to evidence; and it is transferable, sharpening the analysis of arguments, advertisements, speeches, and any use of language. The sections that follow trace where the practice came from and then work systematically through the features of language and form that a close reader learns to notice, before turning to how observations become arguments.

sections.heading: History and Traditions
sections.body: Close reading as a formal practice is largely a product of the twentieth century, though careful attention to texts is far older, rooted in the scholarly interpretation of scripture, law, and the classics, where every word of an authoritative text was weighed. The classical disciplines of rhetoric and philology, the study of persuasive language and of the history and precise meaning of words, supplied habits of textual attention that literary study would inherit. The decisive modern development came in the 1920s and after. In England, the critic I. A. Richards, teaching at Cambridge, conducted experiments in which he gave students poems stripped of their titles and authors and asked them to respond, exposing how badly even educated readers read when deprived of external props. His book Practical Criticism of 1929 argued for training readers to attend to the words on the page themselves. His pupil William Empson, in Seven Types of Ambiguity of 1930, showed through dazzling analyses how the multiple meanings of words enrich poetry, demonstrating the yield of minute verbal attention. In the United States, a related movement called the New Criticism dominated literary study from the 1930s through the 1950s and gave close reading its classic doctrine. Critics such as John Crowe Ransom, who named the movement in a 1941 book, Cleanth Brooks, Robert Penn Warren, W. K. Wimsatt, and Allen Tate insisted that a literary work should be treated as an autonomous, self-contained object, a verbal artifact to be studied in itself, apart from the author's biography and intentions and apart from its effect on readers. Brooks and Warren's influential textbook Understanding Poetry of 1938 taught generations of students to analyze poems through close attention to their internal workings. The New Critics coined warnings that became famous: the intentional fallacy, the error of judging a work by what the author supposedly meant, and the affective fallacy, the error of judging it by the emotions it arouses, both formulated by Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley in the 1940s. They prized irony, paradox, tension, and ambiguity as marks of literary richness, and they treated the poem as, in Brooks's phrase, a well-wrought urn. Later movements challenged the New Criticism's assumptions, especially its treating texts as sealed off from history, politics, and the reader, and literary theory since the 1960s, from structuralism and deconstruction to feminist, Marxist, postcolonial, and historicist criticism, has vastly expanded the questions asked of texts. Yet even these newer approaches depend on close reading as their basic technique; they read texts against the grain, attend to what is unsaid or contradictory, but they still begin with careful attention to language. Close reading, invented as a method by the formalists, outlived the theory that gave it birth and remains the shared foundation of the discipline, the skill that every school of criticism assumes. Understanding this history clarifies both the power and the limits of pure close reading, and prepares the reader to combine textual attention with the broader contexts that later sections restore.

sections.heading: Preparing to Read: Attention and Annotation
sections.body: Close reading begins before any interpretation, with a change of pace and posture toward the text. Where ordinary reading moves quickly and forgets the words as soon as their gist is grasped, close reading is slow, repeated, and physical. The single most important habit is to read the passage more than once, often many times, because meaning and craft reveal themselves gradually. A first reading only establishes what happens; later readings notice how it is written, and later ones still notice why the writing works as it does. The characteristic tool is annotation: marking up the text as one reads, turning a passive scan into an active dialogue with it. Reading with a pen in hand forces attention and leaves a record of observations to work from later. There is no single correct annotation system, but the aim is to register anything that stands out, such as a striking or unexpected word, a repeated pattern, a vivid image, a shift in tone, a break in rhythm, or a puzzling or ambiguous phrase, and to jot questions and hunches in the margins. Underlining, circling, connecting related words with lines, and writing brief notes all serve. Over several readings the marked-up page becomes a map of the text's most active features, and patterns emerge that no single pass would reveal. It helps to work on a copy that can be marked freely, and to give the passage room, since the physical act of annotating is inseparable from the attention it produces. A productive close reading proceeds roughly through the numbered steps below, though in practice they overlap and repeat rather than march in strict order. The reader should cultivate a stance of curiosity rather than mastery, treating puzzles and difficulties not as obstacles but as invitations, since the places where a text resists easy understanding are often where its richest meaning lies. It helps to read aloud at least once, because the ear catches sound, rhythm, and emphasis that the eye slides past, and to notice one's own reactions, such as surprise, confusion, pleasure, or resistance, as clues to what the text is doing and how it is doing it. Above all, the close reader trusts the words, assuming at least provisionally that details are there for a reason and asking of each one what work it performs in the whole. This disciplined attention, sustained over repeated readings and recorded in annotation, is the groundwork on which all the analysis of the following sections is built. Without it, interpretation has nothing solid to stand on; with it, a reader is rarely at a loss for something worth saying about a text, because the page itself, closely attended, is inexhaustibly full of things to notice and to explain.
steps: Read the whole passage once straight through to grasp its literal sense: what happens, who speaks, and what it is about.
Read it again slowly with a pen, marking any word, image, sound, or structural feature that catches your attention or seems significant.
Look up unfamiliar words and check the older or secondary meanings of familiar ones, since writers often exploit a word's full range.
Note patterns and repetitions such as recurring words, images, sounds, or grammatical structures, and mark contrasts, shifts, and anything that seems out of place.
Ask of each striking feature what effect it produces and how it contributes to the passage's meaning or feeling.
Read the passage aloud to hear its rhythm, emphasis, and sound.
Gather your observations, look for connections among them, and form a tentative interpretation of how the parts work together.
Test that interpretation against the details, revising it to account for evidence that does not fit.

sections.heading: Diction and Word Choice
sections.body: The most basic element a close reader attends to is diction: the writer's choice of words. Because a single idea can almost always be expressed in many ways, every word on the page represents a decision, and the particular words chosen carry meanings and overtones that a synonym would not. To read for diction is to ask why this word rather than another, and what the choice reveals or achieves. A useful first distinction is between a word's denotation, its literal dictionary definition, and its connotations, the associations, feelings, and shades of implication it carries beyond that definition. The words childlike and childish both denote qualities of a child, but the first connotes innocence and wonder while the second connotes immaturity and pettiness; a writer choosing between them shapes the reader's judgment. Slender, thin, and scrawny denote roughly the same physical fact but rank from flattering to neutral to unkind. Attending to connotation is often the quickest way into a text's attitude toward its subject. Diction also has a level or register, from high and formal to low and colloquial, from learned and abstract to plain and concrete. A writer may sustain a single register, or may shift deliberately, and such shifts are always worth noticing: a sudden plunge from elevated language into slang, or a rise from the everyday into the grand, marks a change of feeling or a point of emphasis, and sometimes irony. The origin of words matters too, since English draws on both a plain Anglo-Saxon stock and a more formal Latin and Greek one; a passage dense with short Germanic words feels different from one built on long Latinate abstractions. The close reader looks for particular kinds of word choice. Concrete, specific words that name sensory particulars, such as oak rather than tree, or sprinted rather than went, create vividness and precision, while abstract words name ideas and qualities. Unusual, archaic, technical, dialectal, or foreign words stand out and invite the question why they were chosen. Repeated words gain weight through repetition and often mark a text's preoccupations. Words used against their ordinary meaning, or in surprising combinations, generate irony, tension, or fresh perception. Consider a small example: to describe someone who has died, a writer might choose passed away, died, expired, was killed, perished, or croaked, and each carries a different attitude, whether gentle euphemism, plain statement, clinical detachment, violence, elevation, or callous slang. The choice tells us how to feel about the death and often about the speaker. Reading for diction, then, means treating word choice as evidence of meaning and attitude, always asking what a particular word contributes that its alternatives would not. It is among the most reliable and productive of the close reader's habits, because every text, whatever its genre, is made of words, and the words are always chosen. From individual words the reader moves outward to the images and figures those words build, the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: Imagery and Figurative Language
sections.body: Beyond the choice of individual words lies the way words are combined to create images and figures, the pictures a text paints and the imaginative comparisons it makes. Imagery is language that appeals to the senses, evoking sights, sounds, smells, tastes, textures, and sensations of movement and temperature. Though the word suggests the visual, imagery embraces all the senses, and a close reader notes which senses a text engages, how vividly, and to what effect, since concrete sensory detail is much of what makes writing feel alive and particular rather than abstract and general. Figurative language, or figures of speech, uses words in non-literal ways to create meaning and effect. The two central figures are the simile and the metaphor, both of which work by comparison. A simile states a likeness openly, using like or as, as in the road was like a ribbon. A metaphor asserts an identity, describing one thing as if it were another, as in the road was a ribbon, or, more submerged, the ribboning road. Metaphor is arguably the most powerful device in literature and in language generally, because it lets a writer illuminate one thing through the qualities of another, compressing thought and feeling into a single figure and often revealing likeness where none was seen before. A close reader examines what is compared to what, what qualities the comparison transfers, and what it implies: to call a person a lion, a fox, a rock, or a weed says very different things. Related figures extend the repertoire. Personification gives human qualities to nonhuman things, as in the wind whispered or the city never sleeps. Metonymy names something by an associated thing, as the crown stands for the monarchy or the press for journalism, and its close relative synecdoche uses a part for the whole, as hands for workers or wheels for a car. Symbolism lets a concrete thing stand for a larger abstract meaning, as a journey may represent a life or a rose may represent love, though good close reading resists mechanically decoding symbols and attends to how a text builds symbolic weight. Hyperbole exaggerates for effect; understatement, or litotes, deliberately says less than is meant. The close reader attends not only to individual figures but to patterns of imagery across a work. A play or poem may return repeatedly to images of light and dark, of disease, of gardens, or of clothing, and such recurring image-clusters, or motifs, often carry a text's deeper concerns; the imagery of sickness and rot running through Shakespeare's Hamlet is a famous example. When images clash or a metaphor is developed at length into a conceit, as in the elaborate comparisons of the metaphysical poets, the effect repays careful analysis. Reading for imagery and figuration, then, means noticing how a text makes the reader see and sense, what comparisons it draws, and what those comparisons reveal about its subject and its attitude, since a writer's figures are among the surest guides to meaning.

sections.heading: Sound, Rhythm, and Meter
sections.body: Literature is meant to be heard as well as read, and much of its power lies in sound, the music that words make. This is most obvious in poetry, where sound is organized deliberately, but prose too has rhythm and texture, and a close reader learns to listen. Reading aloud is the surest way to notice the features this section describes. Several devices organize the sounds of words. Rhyme, the matching of sounds usually at the ends of lines, binds a poem together, marks its structure, and creates expectation and satisfaction; besides full end rhyme, poets use slant or half rhyme, where the sounds are close but not identical, and internal rhyme within a line. Alliteration is the repetition of initial consonant sounds, as in wild and windy; assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds within words, as in the long o of lonely roads; and consonance repeats consonant sounds elsewhere than at the start. Onomatopoeia uses words whose sound imitates their sense, such as buzz, hiss, or clang. These devices can bind words together, emphasize meaning, slow or quicken the pace, and please the ear, and their absence or disruption is as meaningful as their presence. Rhythm is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line, and in much English poetry it is regularized into meter. The basic unit of meter is the foot, a small group of syllables with a fixed stress pattern. The commonest English foot is the iamb, an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one, as in the word about or the phrase the sun; a line of five iambs is iambic pentameter, the staple of Shakespeare's plays and sonnets and of much English verse, as in the line But soft, what light through yonder window breaks. Other feet include the trochee, stressed then unstressed, as in garden; the anapest, two unstressed then a stressed, giving a galloping motion; and the dactyl, a stressed then two unstressed. Lines are named by the number of feet: trimeter for three, tetrameter for four, and pentameter for five. The close reader scans a line, marking its stressed and unstressed syllables to hear its rhythm, but the deeper interest lies in variation. A poet rarely holds a meter with mechanical strictness; the interest comes from the tension between the expected pattern and the actual speech rhythm, and from deliberate departures. A reversed foot, an extra syllable, or a spondee of two heavy stresses can slow a line, throw weight onto a key word, or mimic the action described. Where the sense runs on past the end of a line without pause, called enjambment, and where a strong pause falls within a line, called a caesura, the movement of thought plays against the shape of the verse. Attending to sound and rhythm, then, means hearing how a text moves and sings, and asking how its music reinforces, complicates, or enacts its meaning, since in the best writing sound and sense are one.

sections.heading: Syntax and Grammar
sections.body: Syntax, the arrangement of words into phrases, clauses, and sentences, is one of the most powerful and most overlooked resources of style, and a close reader learns to attend to sentence structure as carefully as to word choice. Because the same content can be packaged in sentences of very different shapes, the shape a writer chooses controls emphasis, pace, and the reader's experience of the thought as it unfolds. The length and complexity of sentences set a text's basic tempo. Short, simple sentences can convey urgency, plainness, finality, or shock; a string of them creates a clipped, staccato movement. Long, elaborate sentences, with many subordinate clauses, can convey complexity, accumulation, expansiveness, or breathlessness, drawing the reader through a sustained act of thought. A shift from one to the other is always significant: a long, winding sentence broken at last by a short one throws great weight onto the short one. Ernest Hemingway's terse sentences and Henry James's intricate ones represent two poles of syntactic style, each suited to different purposes. The order of elements within a sentence matters as much as its length. English word order is relatively fixed, typically subject, verb, object, so departures from it stand out and gain emphasis. A writer may front a word or phrase for stress, delay the main clause to build suspense, or place the most important idea at the end, the position of greatest weight. A periodic sentence withholds its main point until the close, creating anticipation; a loose, or cumulative, sentence states its main point first and then trails additions. Inversion, reversing normal order, marks emphasis or formality. Repetition and parallelism are among the most noticeable syntactic effects. Parallelism casts related ideas in matching grammatical form, giving balance, rhythm, and force, as in phrases that pair or triple structures of the same shape; it is the backbone of much memorable oratory, as in Lincoln's of the people, by the people, for the people. Repeating a word at the start of successive clauses, called anaphora, hammers a point home. The deliberate omission of conjunctions, or their piling up, speeds or slows the movement and colours the tone. Grammatical choices carry meaning too. The passive voice, which removes or demotes the doer of an action, can create detachment, evasiveness, or a focus on the acted-upon, and its use is often revealing, as when a text says mistakes were made rather than naming who made them. Verb tense and mood, the choice between questions, commands, and statements, and even punctuation, such as the dash that interrupts, the semicolon that balances, and the fragment that arrests, all shape how a sentence is read. Reading for syntax, then, means noticing how sentences are built and asking what their construction does: how it directs emphasis, controls pace, mirrors or resists the thought it carries, and shapes the reader's moment-by-moment experience of the text. Sentence form is meaning in action.

sections.heading: Structure and Form
sections.body: Above the level of the sentence lies the larger architecture of a text: how it is organized, divided, and shaped as a whole. Structure concerns the arrangement of the parts, the order in which things are presented, how they are grouped, and where the divisions and turning points fall, while form concerns the conventional shapes a work may take, such as the sonnet, the tragedy, or the novel. A close reader considers both, since a text's overall design is as expressive as its local detail. In poetry, form is often highly organized and named. The sonnet, a fourteen-line poem in iambic pentameter, comes in two main types whose structure shapes their thought: the Italian, or Petrarchan, sonnet divides into an eight-line octave and a six-line sestet, often posing a problem or question and then answering it, while the English, or Shakespearean, sonnet falls into three four-line quatrains and a final couplet, typically developing an idea in stages and clinching it at the end. The point where a sonnet turns, called the volta, is a structural hinge worth locating. Stanzas group lines as paragraphs group sentences; a refrain repeats; and even open forms without regular meter or rhyme, called free verse, have structure in their arrangement of lines, images, and pauses. In narrative, whether fiction, drama, or epic, structure is the shape of the story's telling. A traditional plot moves through exposition that sets the scene, rising action and complication, a climax or turning point, falling action, and resolution, a pattern the nineteenth-century critic Gustav Freytag diagrammed as a pyramid. But writers manipulate this shape endlessly: beginning in the middle of events, in what classical criticism called in medias res; using flashbacks and foreshadowing; reordering chronology; interweaving multiple plots; or leaving the ending unresolved. The close reader distinguishes the order of events as they happened from the order in which the text reveals them, since the gap between the two is often where meaning and suspense reside. Structure also involves patterns of arrangement that carry meaning: symmetry and balance, repetition with variation, parallel scenes that invite comparison, framing devices in which one story encloses another, and juxtaposition, the significant placing of unlike things side by side. Where a text divides, into acts, chapters, sections, or parts, and how those divisions relate is itself a subject of analysis. Beginnings and endings deserve special attention, since the first words establish expectations and the last words leave the final impression and often reveal the design of the whole. Reading for structure, then, means stepping back from the individual word and sentence to ask how the parts are ordered and shaped, how the beginning leads to the end, where the turns and divisions fall, and how the overall form supports or complicates the meaning. The largest patterns of a work, no less than its smallest verbal details, are chosen, and the close reader asks what those choices accomplish.

sections.heading: Tone, Voice, and Point of View
sections.body: Every text has a tone, an attitude toward its subject and its reader, and much of close reading aims to discern it, since tone colours everything and is often the key to a text's meaning. Tone is the emotional and evaluative stance a text conveys: it may be earnest, ironic, playful, mournful, bitter, tender, detached, or indignant, and any of countless shades, and it is produced by the combined effect of diction, imagery, syntax, sound, and detail. Because tone is rarely announced outright, the close reader infers it from the evidence, asking how a text seems to feel about what it describes, and watching for shifts, since a change of tone marks a change of meaning or feeling. Irony deserves particular attention, because it is the figure in which tone and literal statement diverge, and misreading it is among the commonest failures of interpretation. In verbal irony a speaker says one thing and means another, often the opposite, as when a calamity is called splendid; the reader must catch the gap between the words and the intended meaning. Dramatic irony, in narrative and drama, occurs when the reader knows something a character does not, giving the character's words a second, unintended significance. Situational irony arises when events turn out contrary to expectation. Sustained irony can pervade a whole work, as in satire, where an entire text says the reverse of what it means in order to expose folly, as in Jonathan Swift's A Modest Proposal of 1729, which coolly recommends eating children to attack the callousness of the age. Voice is the distinctive personality that seems to speak in a text, its characteristic manner, its habits of word and rhythm, and the sense of a particular sensibility behind the words. A close reader must distinguish the author from the speaker or narrator, since the voice that speaks in a poem or story is a construction and may differ sharply from the writer. In poetry the speaker may be a persona quite unlike the poet; the ranting duke who speaks Robert Browning's My Last Duchess condemns himself in words Browning has crafted for the purpose. Point of view, in narrative, is the position from which a story is told, and it powerfully shapes what the reader knows and feels. A first-person narrator tells the story as I, giving intimacy but limited and possibly unreliable knowledge; the close reader is alert to the unreliable narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted. A third-person narrator tells the story from outside; such a narrator may be omniscient, knowing all minds and events, or limited to a single character's perspective. The choice governs sympathy, irony, and access to truth. Reading for tone, voice, and point of view, then, means asking who speaks, from what position, with what attitude, and how far to trust them, questions that determine how the whole text is to be taken.

sections.heading: Theme and Meaning
sections.body: Beyond describing how a text works, close reading aims finally at what it means, at its themes, the central ideas and concerns it explores. A theme is not the same as a subject or a topic, and the distinction is important. The subject of a work is what it is about in a word or two, such as love, war, ambition, or growing up, while the theme is what the work says or suggests about that subject, the insight or vision it offers. Love is a subject; the idea that love and possessiveness are hard to separate is a theme. A theme is best stated as a full thought, a claim the text seems to make or a question it raises, not a single word. Theme is not a hidden moral tucked inside a text, waiting to be extracted so that the story can then be discarded, nor is it usually stated outright; it emerges from everything the close reader has learned to notice, including the pattern of imagery, the arc of the plot, the choices of diction and tone, the fate of the characters, and the shape of the form. To arrive at theme, the reader gathers observations and asks what larger concern they add up to, what the accumulated details are exploring. A recurring image of cages and confinement across a novel, the failure of a character's attempts at freedom, and a syntax that hems the prose in may together point to a theme about the limits of individual liberty. Theme is thus the destination of close reading, reached by way of the text's concrete features rather than imposed on them. Good interpretation of theme observes several cautions. Great literary works rarely reduce to a single tidy message; they hold ideas in tension, explore rather than assert, and often leave questions open, so the richest thematic statements acknowledge complexity and ambiguity rather than flattening the work into a slogan. A text may entertain contradictory possibilities without resolving them, and honouring that irresolution is truer reading than forcing a verdict. Interpretation must also stay grounded: a claim about theme is persuasive only insofar as it is supported by the text's details, and a reading that the words cannot bear, however ingenious, is a misreading. There is seldom a single correct interpretation, but interpretations are not all equal; they are better or worse according to how fully and precisely they account for the evidence. The relation between the parts and the whole is central. Individual observations gain significance as they connect to a larger understanding, and the larger understanding is tested and refined against the parts, in a movement back and forth that interpreters call the hermeneutic circle. Reading for theme, then, means synthesizing everything the close reading has revealed into an account of what the text explores and suggests, the point at which noticing becomes understanding.

sections.heading: From Observation to Argument
sections.body: Close reading generates observations; literary analysis turns them into an argument. The two are distinct, and learning to make the passage from one to the other is what separates a list of noticed details from a genuine interpretation. An essay of literary analysis does not merely report what a text contains or how a reader feels about it; it advances a claim about the text's meaning or workings and supports that claim with evidence and reasoning drawn from the text itself. At the centre of an analytical essay is a thesis: a specific, arguable claim about the text that the essay will demonstrate. A strong thesis is not a statement of fact that no one would dispute, nor a summary of the plot, nor a mere observation; it is an interpretation that a reasonable person might contest and that the essay must therefore argue for. That the poem uses metaphor is an observation; that the poem's metaphors of enclosure work against its stated theme of freedom, revealing a deeper ambivalence, is a thesis. The thesis answers a so-what question, telling the reader not just what is in the text but why it matters and what it means. The body of the analysis supports the thesis through the disciplined use of textual evidence. Evidence in literary study is quotation and precise reference to the text, the actual words, images, structures, and devices that the close reading has identified. But evidence does not speak for itself; it must be analyzed. The characteristic move of literary argument is to quote a specific detail and then explain how it supports the claim, to show, not merely assert, the connection between the observed feature and the interpretive point. A common failure is to quote and move on, assuming the significance is obvious; the analytical work lies precisely in the explanation that links the evidence to the argument, unpacking how the language produces the effect claimed. An effective analysis is selective and focused rather than exhaustive. It does not catalogue every device in the text but chooses the observations that bear on its thesis and arranges them into a coherent line of reasoning, each paragraph advancing one aspect of the argument. It anticipates and addresses evidence that complicates the claim, since acknowledging tension and counter-evidence strengthens an interpretation rather than weakening it, and honesty about a text's difficulties is a mark of good criticism. The process usually runs backward from the finished essay's order: the reader first reads closely and gathers observations, then notices patterns and connections among them, then forms a tentative interpretation, and only then shapes that interpretation into a thesis and marshals the evidence to support it, discarding what does not serve the argument. Writing itself often clarifies the interpretation, as the effort to explain forces vague impressions into precise claims. Analysis, then, is close reading made into argument: observation disciplined by evidence, reasoning, and the obligation to persuade.

sections.heading: Critical Lenses and Theoretical Approaches
sections.body: Pure close reading treats a text as a self-contained object, but since the mid-twentieth century literary study has developed a range of theoretical approaches, often called critical lenses, that bring particular questions and contexts to bear on a text. Each lens directs attention to certain features and asks certain questions, and while they can be used dogmatically, at their best they enrich close reading by expanding what a reader thinks to notice. They do not replace close attention to language; they give it direction. Formalist criticism, including the New Criticism from which close reading grew, focuses on the text itself, its language, structure, and devices, largely apart from history, biography, and the reader, and it remains the approach most fully identified with close reading. Reader-response criticism shifts attention to the reader's active role in making meaning, holding that a text is realized only in the act of reading and that different readers legitimately construct it differently. Historical and biographical approaches restore the contexts the formalists set aside, reading a text in relation to the life of its author and the circumstances of its time. The movement known as New Historicism, prominent since the 1980s, reads literary works alongside other documents of their period, treating literature as bound up with the power relations and discourses of its historical moment. Several lenses read for politics and power. Marxist criticism examines how a text reflects and engages the economic and class structures of its society, attending to who has power and wealth and how the text represents or masks social conflict. Feminist criticism examines how texts represent gender, how they reflect or challenge the subordination of women, and how a work's meaning shifts when read with attention to sex and gender; gender and queer theory extend this to the construction of sexuality and identity. Postcolonial criticism examines literature in relation to empire, colonialism, and their aftermath, attending to how texts represent colonized peoples and how writers from formerly colonized societies respond. Psychoanalytic criticism, drawing on Freud and later theorists, reads for unconscious desires, conflicts, and symbolism in characters, authors, and texts. Structuralism seeks the underlying systems and codes, modelled on language, that generate meaning, while its successor, deconstruction, associated with Jacques Derrida, reads texts against themselves to expose the instabilities, contradictions, and undecidable meanings in their language, challenging the idea that a text has a single settled meaning. No single lens is simply correct, and skilled critics often combine them, choosing the questions that a particular text and purpose make fruitful. The lenses are tools, not doctrines: a reader uses them to see more, not to force a text into a predetermined verdict. For the close reader, the value of theory lies in the fresh questions it supplies, about power, gender, history, the unconscious, the reader, and the instability of language, which send one back to the words with sharper eyes.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls and Where It Connects
sections.body: Close reading is a demanding skill, and certain errors recur often enough to be worth naming. The first and most basic is confusing summary with analysis: retelling what a text says or what happens in a story, rather than examining how it works and what it means. Summary reports content; analysis interprets and argues. A reader who has merely paraphrased the plot has not yet begun to read closely, however accurate the paraphrase. A second pitfall is unsupported assertion, making claims about a text's meaning without grounding them in its details. Interpretation must be tied to evidence in the words on the page; a reading that floats free of the text, however clever, is mere assertion. The opposite error is the pointless collection of detail, cataloguing devices and features without connecting them to any larger interpretive point, so that the reading becomes a list rather than an argument. Observation and interpretation must work together, each serving the other. A third danger is over-reading: forcing significance onto every detail, decoding symbols the text will not bear, or building elaborate interpretations on slender evidence. Not every red object is a symbol of passion, and a disciplined reader distinguishes what the text supports from what an ingenious mind can impose. The related fault of reading in a predetermined conclusion, deciding what a text must mean and then hunting for evidence, betrays the openness that close reading requires. Good reading follows the evidence rather than commanding it. A fourth is the confusion of the author with the speaker or narrator, treating a poem's I or a novel's narrator as the direct voice of the writer, and so missing irony, persona, and unreliability. A fifth is misjudging tone, especially failing to detect irony and taking as sincere what is meant sardonically, or the reverse. And a recurring temptation is to substitute external information, such as the author's biography, historical facts, or received opinion about a work, for engagement with the text itself; context can illuminate, but it cannot replace the reading it is meant to serve. Awareness of these pitfalls sharpens practice, and the remedy for all of them is the same: return to the words, ask what they actually support, and hold interpretation answerable to evidence. Close reading connects outward to much beyond the study of literature. As a discipline of careful attention to language, it sharpens the critical reading of any text, including arguments, journalism, advertising, political speech, law, and scripture, wherever the exact wording carries weight and where noticing how something is said reveals its purposes. It underlies the teaching of writing, since understanding how effects are achieved helps one achieve them. It joins with linguistics in the study of language, with history and philosophy in the interpretation of documents, and with rhetoric in the analysis of persuasion. Above all it cultivates a habit of mind, patient, curious, and evidence-bound attention, that is among the most transferable and durable rewards of a literary education.

guides.title: Literary Theory & the Schools of Criticism
guides.summary: A survey of how literature has been read and interpreted, from classical poetics through formalism, structuralism, and deconstruction to psychoanalytic, Marxist, feminist, postcolonial, and ecological criticism, with the questions each school asks of a text.

sections.heading: What Literary Theory Is and What It Does
sections.body: Literary theory is the systematic reflection on what literature is, how it means, and how it should be read. It stands one step back from ordinary reading and even from ordinary criticism: where a critic interprets a particular poem or novel, the theorist asks what interpretation itself involves, what makes a text literary, where meaning resides, and what a reader is doing when she reads. These questions sound abstract, but they have direct consequences, because how you answer them determines what you notice in a book and what you take a reading to be for. A reader who believes meaning lies in the author's intention will read to recover what the writer meant; one who believes meaning is produced by the reader will attend to her own response; one who believes texts are shaped by class conflict, or by the unconscious, or by structures of language beyond anyone's control, will look for those forces at work. Theory thus supplies the assumptions, often unexamined, behind every act of interpretation, and studying it makes those assumptions visible and open to argument. It is useful to distinguish several recurring questions that organize the whole field. The first concerns the source of meaning: does a text mean what its author intended, what its words say independent of any author, what a reader makes of it, or what the historical and social conditions of its making determined? The second concerns the object of study: is the proper focus the individual work as a self-contained artifact, the system of conventions that makes it possible, the psychology of its creator or reader, or the social and material world it reflects and shapes? The third concerns the purpose of criticism: is it to appreciate beauty, to evaluate quality, to recover historical meaning, to expose hidden ideologies, or to change how we see the world? Different schools of criticism are, in large part, different answers to these questions, each illuminating some aspect of literature while neglecting others. It is a mistake to think of them as a simple progression in which later theories refute earlier ones; rather, they are competing and sometimes complementary lenses, and a sophisticated reader learns to use several. Literary theory drew much of its modern energy from neighboring disciplines, linguistics, psychoanalysis, Marxism, anthropology, philosophy, and its history in the twentieth century is partly the story of literature departments absorbing and adapting ideas from these fields, sometimes to the point of controversy about whether theory had displaced literature itself. This guide surveys the major schools in roughly the order they arose, showing what each contributed, what it left out, and how the whole conversation bears on the practical act of reading a text with understanding. The aim is not to convert the reader to any single theory but to equip her to see how meaning is made and contested.

sections.heading: Classical and Pre-Modern Criticism: Mimesis to Rhetoric
sections.body: Reflection on literature is as old as literature itself, and the categories the ancient world devised still underlie modern debate. In Greece the central idea was mimesis, imitation or representation: literature was understood as an imitation of human life and action. Plato, in the Republic, treated this suspiciously. If the world of appearances is already a copy of the eternal Forms, then art, imitating appearances, is a copy of a copy, twice removed from reality, and Plato worried that poetry stirs the emotions and spreads falsehoods about the gods, leading him to banish most poets from his ideal city. His pupil Aristotle answered this indictment in the Poetics, the founding work of Western literary theory, written in the fourth century BCE. Aristotle defended imitation as natural and instructive, and he analyzed tragedy with an anatomist's precision, identifying its parts, plot, character, thought, diction, melody, and spectacle, and ranking plot as the soul of tragedy. He argued that a well-constructed tragedy arouses pity and fear and achieves catharsis, a purging or clarification of these emotions, and he formulated influential concepts still in use: the tragic hero of high standing brought down not by vice but by an error or flaw, the reversal of fortune, the moment of recognition, and the unity of a plot whose events follow one another by necessity or probability. Where Plato saw danger, Aristotle saw form and function, and his empirical, formal approach set a lasting precedent. The Roman inheritance shifted the emphasis toward rhetoric and craft. Horace, in his verse epistle known as the Art of Poetry, offered practical counsel and the enduring formula that poetry should both delight and instruct, giving pleasure while teaching, and he prized decorum, the fitting of style to subject. The treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus, explored how great writing transports and overwhelms the reader through elevation of thought and intensity of language, introducing an aesthetics of grandeur beyond mere correctness. Through late antiquity and the Middle Ages, literary reflection was largely bound up with rhetoric, grammar, and the interpretation of sacred scripture, where the practice of reading texts on multiple levels, literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical, refined techniques of interpretation that would outlast their theological origin. The Renaissance revived classical poetics, and defenders of poetry such as Philip Sidney, in his Apology for Poetry, answered Puritan attacks by arguing that the poet, unbound by mere fact, can deliver a golden world more instructive than nature's brazen one, teaching virtue more movingly than the philosopher or historian. This long tradition established the questions and vocabulary, imitation, form, genre, emotional effect, the union of pleasure and instruction, decorum, the sublime, that later criticism would inherit, contest, and transform, and it treated literature as a serious art with rules, purposes, and power over the soul.

sections.heading: Romantic and Nineteenth-Century Criticism
sections.body: The late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries brought a profound reorientation in how literature was conceived, a shift the critic M. H. Abrams described as the move from the mirror to the lamp. Where classical and neoclassical theory had treated the poem as a mirror held up to nature, an imitation of the external world governed by rules of craft, the Romantics treated it as a lamp, a projection of the poet's inner life, feeling, and imagination. The emphasis moved from the object represented to the creating subject. William Wordsworth, in the preface to Lyrical Ballads in 1800, a manifesto of English Romanticism, defined poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, taking its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity, and he rejected the artificial poetic diction of his predecessors in favor of the real language of ordinary people. Samuel Taylor Coleridge supplied the movement's deepest theory, distinguishing the imagination, a living, creative, unifying power that fuses disparate elements into organic wholes, from the mere fancy, which only reassembles fixed materials; he described the willing suspension of disbelief that poetic faith requires and conceived the literary work as an organic form growing from within like a living thing, rather than a mechanical arrangement of parts. This organic conception, the poem as a self-developing unity in which every element is necessary to the whole, would prove enormously influential. Percy Shelley, in his Defence of Poetry, made grand claims for the moral and political power of imagination, arguing that poets, by enlarging our sympathies, are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. The Romantic elevation of genius, originality, imagination, and feeling reshaped the very idea of the author, from a skilled craftsman working within conventions to an inspired individual expressing a unique vision. Later in the century, criticism took several directions. Matthew Arnold, an influential Victorian critic, gave criticism a lofty cultural mission: he defined it as a disinterested endeavor to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world, and he looked to literature, in an age of waning religious faith, to sustain culture and moral seriousness, judging poetry by touchstones of the highest quality. A contrary current, the aestheticism of Walter Pater and the art for art's sake movement, rejected such moralism, insisting that art exists for its own sake and that the proper response to a work is intense, discriminating appreciation of its beauty rather than any moral or social lesson. Meanwhile the rise of realism in fiction prompted its own reflection on how novels represent society and character truthfully. Nineteenth-century criticism thus bequeathed to the modern era a rich but unstable legacy: the exaltation of imagination and the author's inner life, the ideal of the organic unity of the work, the claim that literature carries moral and cultural authority, and the opposing claim that it answers only to beauty, tensions that the theoretical revolutions of the twentieth century would confront directly.

sections.heading: Russian Formalism and the Question of Literariness
sections.body: Modern literary theory in the strict sense begins in the second decade of the twentieth century with a group of Russian scholars who sought to make the study of literature a genuine science with its own object. The Russian Formalists, working in Moscow and in the group known as the Petersburg society for the study of poetic language from around 1915, rejected the reigning approaches that treated literature as a window onto the author's biography, the nation's spirit, or social conditions. They asked instead what makes a verbal work literary at all, and they named their object literariness, the quality that distinguishes literary language from ordinary language. Their answer centered on form and technique rather than content or reference. Ordinary language, they argued, is practical and transparent; we look through it to its message and cease to notice the words themselves. Literary language, by contrast, is self-conscious, foregrounding its own devices, its sounds, rhythms, patterns, and structures, so that the medium becomes palpable. Viktor Shklovsky formulated the movement's most famous concept, ostranenie, usually translated as defamiliarization or estrangement: the function of art, he argued, is to make the familiar strange, to slow down and complicate perception so that we experience things freshly rather than recognizing them automatically. Habit deadens perception, and the techniques of art, by roughening form and delaying understanding, restore the sensation of life. On this view the content of a work, the story it tells, matters less than the devices by which it is told, and Shklovsky provocatively analyzed how a novel's digressions and delays are not obstacles to the story but the very substance of its art. The Formalists distinguished, in narrative, between the fabula, the raw chronological sequence of events, and the sjuzhet, the arrangement in which those events are actually presented in the text, a distinction fundamental to the later study of narrative; a plot's artistry lies largely in how it reorders, withholds, and reveals. In the study of verse, they analyzed sound patterning, meter, and the interplay of rhythm and syntax as the machinery of poetic effect. Roman Jakobson, who bridged Russian Formalism and later structuralism, sought to define the poetic function of language precisely, arguing that it consists in projecting the principle of equivalence from the axis of selection onto the axis of combination, meaning that in poetry, elements that are merely similar, in sound or grammar, are set in sequence, so that likeness in rhyme, meter, and parallelism becomes the organizing principle of the message. The Formalists were suppressed under Soviet ideological pressure by the early 1930s, condemned for ignoring the social content of literature, but their ideas survived through émigrés and through the Prague School, and they laid the groundwork for structuralism, narratology, and the whole modern concern with the specifically literary properties of texts. Their lasting contribution was to insist that criticism attend to how a work is made, treating literature as a craft of language with analyzable techniques rather than a mere vehicle for biography or ideas.

sections.heading: New Criticism and Close Reading
sections.body: In the English-speaking world, the dominant approach to literature from roughly the 1930s through the 1950s was the New Criticism, a movement centered in the United States and Britain that transformed how literature was taught and read. Like the Russian Formalists, whom they resembled without direct influence, the New Critics insisted that the poem itself, its words on the page, is the proper object of study, and they resisted the tendency to reduce a work to its author's biography, its historical background, or its emotional effect on readers. Their positive method was close reading, the patient, detailed analysis of the language of a text, attending to its imagery, ambiguity, irony, paradox, tension, and structure, on the conviction that a poem is a complex verbal artifact whose meaning is embodied in the precise interplay of its words and cannot be paraphrased without loss. Cleanth Brooks called this the heresy of paraphrase, the mistake of thinking a poem's meaning can be restated in other words; the poem means what it is, an organized structure of tensions resolved into unity. The New Critics prized the well-wrought urn, the poem as a self-sufficient whole whose apparent contradictions are held in balance, and they especially admired the metaphysical poets and any verse rich in irony and ambiguity. William Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity demonstrated how much interpretive richness careful attention to multiple meanings could yield, while I. A. Richards pioneered practical criticism by showing how unreliably even trained readers judged poems stripped of their authors' names, arguing for disciplined, text-focused reading. The theoretical backbone of the movement was supplied in two influential essays by W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley. The intentional fallacy warns against judging a work by reference to the author's intention, which is neither available nor decisive; what matters is what the words actually achieve, not what the writer meant to do. The affective fallacy warns against confusing the poem with its emotional effects on the reader, which vary and cannot ground objective interpretation. Together these arguments sealed the text off from both author and reader, locating meaning firmly in the verbal object itself. The New Criticism had enormous pedagogical value, for it gave students and teachers a portable technique, close reading, that required no specialized historical knowledge and could be applied to any text, and it professionalized literary study. But its limitations drew increasing criticism. By treating the poem as a timeless, autonomous artifact, it tended to ignore history, politics, and the social conditions of literature; by focusing on short lyric poems suited to close analysis, it was less at home with long novels and their sprawling engagement with society; and its claim of objectivity concealed value judgments about which works were worth studying. Later theory would reopen everything the New Criticism had closed off, the author, the reader, history, ideology, but the discipline of close reading it perfected remains an indispensable skill, and even critics who reject its premises still practice the careful attention to language it taught.

sections.heading: Structuralism and Narratology
sections.body: Structuralism was the most ambitious theoretical movement of the mid-twentieth century, and it applied to literature and culture the model of language developed by Ferdinand de Saussure. Saussure had argued that a language is a system in which signs have meaning not in themselves but through their differences from other signs, and that the proper study is of the underlying system, langue, rather than individual utterances, parole. Structuralists generalized this insight into a method for analyzing any system of signs, holding that the meaning of any cultural element, a word, a gesture, a dish, a fashion, a story, derives from its place within a structure of relations and oppositions. The anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss applied the model to myth, arguing that beneath the endless diversity of myths lie a small number of underlying structures built from binary oppositions, such as raw and cooked or nature and culture, which the myth works to mediate; the individual myth is a variation on deep patterns the analyst can uncover. In literary study this program produced narratology, the systematic science of narrative, which seeks the universal grammar underlying all stories. An early inspiration was Vladimir Propp, a Russian scholar who, analyzing a corpus of folktales, found that beneath their varied surfaces lay a fixed sequence of a limited set of functions, actions defined by their role in the plot, such as the hero leaving home, being tested, or defeating a villain, always occurring in the same order though not all present in every tale. Later narratologists such as A. J. Greimas, Tzvetan Todorov, Roland Barthes in his structuralist phase, and above all Gérard Genette built elaborate frameworks for describing how narratives work. Genette distinguished with great precision the levels of narrative: the order in which events are told versus the order in which they happen, allowing analysis of flashback and anticipation; the duration and frequency of narration; the difference between who sees, the focalizer, and who speaks, the narrator; and the various relations between narrator and story. Structuralist poetics, exemplified by Jonathan Culler's account, shifted attention from interpreting individual works to describing the system of conventions, the literary competence, that enables readers to make sense of texts at all, asking not what a poem means but how it comes to be readable as a poem. The appeal of structuralism was its promise of rigor and objectivity, a genuine science of literature grounded in the analysis of systems rather than the impressions of individual critics, and its influence spread across the humanities and social sciences. Its limitations, however, prompted the reaction that followed. In seeking timeless underlying structures, it tended to neglect history, change, and the individual work's particularity; in treating the human subject as merely a position within a system, it seemed to dissolve the author and the reader into anonymous structures; and its confidence that structures could be objectively identified would soon be challenged by thinkers who had begun within structuralism itself and turned against its assumptions.

sections.heading: Post-Structuralism and Deconstruction
sections.body: Post-structuralism emerged in France in the late 1960s from within structuralism, accepting its starting point, that meaning is produced by systems of signs rather than by things or intentions, but radicalizing it to undermine the stability structuralism had sought. If, as Saussure held, signs mean only through their differences from other signs, the post-structuralists argued, then meaning is never fully present in any sign but is endlessly deferred along chains of signification, and the structuralist dream of pinning down fixed underlying structures collapses. The central figure is Jacques Derrida, whose method of reading, deconstruction, he introduced in works published around 1967. Derrida argued that Western thought has been governed by a metaphysics of presence that privileges speech over writing and craves a stable center or ground of meaning, and that it organizes itself through hierarchical binary oppositions, presence over absence, speech over writing, nature over culture, man over woman, in which the first term is treated as primary and the second as derivative or deficient. Deconstruction shows that these hierarchies are unstable: close reading reveals that the privileged term secretly depends on the subordinate one, that the oppositions cannot be maintained, and that texts undermine their own apparent claims. He coined the term différance, playing on the French for both to differ and to defer, to name the way meaning is generated by differences and perpetually postponed, never arriving at a final signified. His often-quoted assertion that there is nothing outside the text is best understood not as a denial of reality but as the claim that we have no access to meaning except through the endless play of signification, with no anchoring point outside language that would halt interpretation. In the United States, deconstruction was taken up by critics associated with Yale, notably Paul de Man, who argued that literary language is fundamentally rhetorical and figurative, so that every text contains contradictions between what it says and what it does, between its grammatical and its rhetorical dimensions, making any final, coherent interpretation impossible; reading, on this view, is the discovery of a text's inevitable undecidability. Post-structuralism was not only Derrida. Roland Barthes, moving beyond his structuralist phase, proclaimed the death of the author, arguing that a text is not a message from an originating author to be decoded but a tissue of quotations drawn from innumerable sources of culture, whose unity lies in its destination, the reader, not its origin; meaning is produced in reading, not deposited by writing. This dethroning of the author and of stable meaning was liberating and disturbing in equal measure. Critics charged that deconstruction, by making every text undecidable and denying any ground for interpretation, led to relativism and interpretive paralysis, and that its intricate wordplay could become an end in itself. Defenders replied that it fosters a rigorous humility about the limits of interpretation and a heightened attention to the workings of language, exposing the hidden assumptions and suppressed contradictions in texts and in the very concepts, truth, presence, origin, that other theories take for granted. Whatever one concludes, post-structuralism permanently unsettled the confident objectivity of both structuralism and the New Criticism.

sections.heading: Psychoanalytic Criticism
sections.body: Psychoanalytic criticism reads literature through the theories of the unconscious mind developed by Sigmund Freud and his successors, on the premise that literary works, like dreams, jokes, and slips of the tongue, express desires and conflicts that are hidden from conscious awareness. Freud held that the mind is divided, that much of mental life is unconscious, and that repressed wishes, especially those arising in early childhood and often sexual in nature, return in disguised form. Because art resembles the disguised fulfillment of a wish, literature offered Freud a natural field, and he himself analyzed works, most famously reading the myth of Oedipus and Shakespeare's Hamlet in terms of the Oedipus complex, the child's forbidden desire for the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the same-sex parent, arguing that Hamlet's paralysis expresses his own repressed guilt. Early psychoanalytic criticism took several forms. One approach treated the literary work as a symptom of its author's psyche, reading the text to uncover the writer's neuroses and repressed conflicts, an approach vulnerable to the objection that it reduces art to biography and treats characters as if they were real patients. A second approach analyzed characters within the work as psychological cases, illuminating their motives through concepts such as repression, projection, and the unconscious. A third, more defensible approach attends to the reader's psychology, asking how literature engages the unconscious desires and fears of its audience, why we take pleasure in tragedy or horror, and how identification and fantasy operate in reading. The most influential reworking of psychoanalysis for literary theory came from the French analyst Jacques Lacan, who reinterpreted Freud through the lens of structural linguistics, declaring that the unconscious is structured like a language. Lacan's account of the mirror stage describes how the infant forms an illusory sense of a unified self by identifying with its image, so that the ego is founded on a misrecognition; and his distinction among three registers, the imaginary, the symbolic, the order of language and law into which we are inducted, and the real, that which resists symbolization, gave critics a rich vocabulary. For Lacan desire is bound up with language and with a fundamental lack that can never be filled, and the subject is decentered, not master in its own house, an idea that converged with post-structuralism's suspicion of the unified self. Later theorists combined psychoanalysis with feminism and film theory; the concept of the gaze, developed in Laura Mulvey's analysis of how cinema positions the spectator and objectifies the female figure, drew on Lacanian ideas to political effect. Psychoanalytic criticism has been sharply contested. Skeptics question the scientific standing of psychoanalysis itself, warn against the circularity of an interpretation that can explain any evidence and its opposite, and object that finding phallic symbols and Oedipal patterns everywhere can become a mechanical exercise that flattens the specificity of works. Yet at its best the approach takes seriously that literature moves us at levels below conscious understanding, that reading can be an encounter with what we do not fully know about desire, loss, and the self, making it a durable, if disputed, resource of criticism.

sections.heading: Marxist and Materialist Criticism
sections.body: Marxist criticism reads literature in relation to the economic and social conditions that produce it, insisting that art is not a timeless expression of universal human nature but a product of history, shaped by the material realities of its age and by the conflicts among social classes. Its foundation is Karl Marx's claim that the economic base of a society, its mode of production and the relations of ownership and labor it entails, conditions the superstructure of law, politics, religion, philosophy, and art, so that the ideas and cultural forms of an era tend to reflect and serve the interests of its dominant class. From this follows the concept of ideology, understood as the ways in which a society's beliefs, including those embodied in literature, present the particular interests of the ruling class as natural, universal, and inevitable, and thereby help reproduce an unjust order. Marxist critics therefore ask what a literary work reveals, often unintentionally, about the class relations and ideological assumptions of its time: whose interests its values serve, what it makes visible and what it silently excludes, how its very form encodes a social vision. The tradition is rich and internally varied. Georg Lukács, a Hungarian critic, championed the realist novel of the nineteenth century for its capacity to represent the totality of social relations and to show individuals as historically situated types, and he criticized modernist fragmentation as a symptom of alienation. Against him, Bertolt Brecht argued for an anti-illusionist art that breaks the spell of realism, using devices of estrangement to make the audience think critically about social conditions rather than lose themselves in the story. The Frankfurt School theorists Theodor Adorno and Walter Benjamin explored the fate of art under capitalism from opposed angles: Adorno defended difficult, autonomous modern art as a refuge of critical negativity against the deadening culture industry of mass entertainment, while Benjamin, more hopefully, examined how mechanical reproduction, in film and photography, might strip art of its aura and open new political possibilities. The French Marxist Louis Althusser reconceived ideology not as false consciousness but as the imaginary relationship of individuals to their real conditions, a system that hails or interpellates individuals as subjects and that operates through institutions, and his ideas shaped a generation of critics, including Pierre Macherey, who argued that a text's significant silences and gaps reveal the ideological contradictions it cannot openly express. The most influential figure in Anglophone Marxist criticism, Fredric Jameson, urged critics always to historicize and analyzed how narrative form itself carries a political unconscious, encoding and managing the social contradictions of its moment. Marxist criticism has been faulted for sometimes reducing complex works to reflections of economic conditions, for subordinating aesthetic value to political judgment, and for the failures of the regimes that invoked Marx, and later Marxists took pains to grant art a relative autonomy rather than treat it as a mere mirror of the base. Yet the tradition permanently enriched criticism by insisting that literature is embedded in history and power, that form and ideology are inseparable, and that reading can expose the social interests hidden within apparently innocent stories.

sections.heading: Feminist, Gender, and Queer Theory
sections.body: Feminist criticism, which emerged as a major force with the women's movement of the late 1960s and 1970s, reads literature with attention to gender, exposing how texts and the traditions that canonize them have represented, marginalized, and been shaped by women, and challenging the assumption that a supposedly universal, neutral perspective is in fact a male one. Its concerns are several. One is critique of the representation of women in works by men, analyzing the stereotypes, the angel and the monster, the virgin and the whore, and the ways literature has encoded patriarchal attitudes; Kate Millett's Sexual Politics offered an early, combative example, reading canonical male authors for their sexual ideology. A second concern is the recovery of women writers unjustly neglected by a male-dominated canon, and the study of a distinct female literary tradition; Elaine Showalter named this project gynocriticism, the study of women as writers, their history, themes, and forms, and Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar, in The Madwoman in the Attic, influentially examined the anxieties and strategies of nineteenth-century women writers working within and against a patriarchal tradition, reading the rebellious madwoman as the author's double. A foundational text behind all this was Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, which argued that women's literary achievement had been constrained by material conditions, the lack of money, education, and independent space, and imagined the thwarted fate of a hypothetical sister of Shakespeare. French feminist theory, drawing on psychoanalysis and post-structuralism, took a different path: Hélène Cixous and Luce Irigaray explored the idea of a specifically feminine writing that might escape the masculine structures of language, while Julia Kristeva analyzed the disruptive, pre-symbolic dimension of language. A crucial development was the distinction between biological sex and socially constructed gender, and the recognition, pressed by Black feminists such as bell hooks and by the concept of intersectionality named by Kimberlé Crenshaw, that gender cannot be analyzed in isolation from race, class, and sexuality, since women's experiences differ profoundly across these axes. From these roots grew gender studies and queer theory, which extended the analysis to sexuality and to the very categories of male and female, gay and straight. Judith Butler's Gender Trouble argued that gender is not the expression of a prior inner essence but is performatively produced, constituted through repeated stylized acts that create the illusion of a natural, stable identity, a claim that destabilized the notion of fixed sexual identity itself. Queer theory, drawing also on Michel Foucault's history of sexuality, which argued that the homosexual as a type of person was a relatively recent historical construction rather than a timeless natural kind, and on Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's analysis of how the hetero-homosexual distinction structures modern culture, reads literature for the instability of sexual categories and for desires and identities that exceed the normative. These interlocking approaches transformed the discipline, reshaping the canon, the questions asked of texts, and the understanding that gender and sexuality are not natural givens but constructed, contested, and inscribed in the language and forms of literature.

sections.heading: Postcolonial Criticism
sections.body: Postcolonial criticism examines literature in relation to the history of European colonialism and its aftermath, analyzing how colonized peoples were represented, how imperial power shaped culture and knowledge, and how writers from formerly colonized societies have contested and rewritten the inherited traditions. Its founding text is Edward Said's Orientalism of 1978, which analyzed the vast body of Western scholarship, literature, and art about the East and argued that Orientalism was not neutral knowledge but a discourse, in Foucault's sense, that produced the Orient as an exotic, irrational, backward Other against which the West defined itself as rational and superior, and that this discourse was bound up with, and helped justify, imperial domination. Said showed that even canonical European literature was implicated in empire, and his method, reading texts for the assumptions and power relations of colonialism, opened a new field. Two other theorists shaped its dominant form. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, translating Derrida and combining deconstruction, Marxism, and feminism, posed in a famous essay the question of whether the subaltern, the most oppressed and voiceless colonized subject, especially the colonized woman, can speak, or whether they are always spoken for and represented by others, warning against the intellectual's presumption to give them voice. Homi Bhabha, drawing on psychoanalysis and post-structuralism, developed concepts that complicate the simple opposition of colonizer and colonized: hybridity, the mixed, in-between cultural identities produced in the colonial encounter; mimicry, the way the colonized are encouraged to imitate the colonizer yet, being almost the same but not quite, produce a menacing, subversive difference; and the ambivalence at the heart of colonial authority. Behind these academic theorists stood earlier anticolonial writers, notably Frantz Fanon, whose analyses of the psychology of colonization, the internalized inferiority it induces and the role of violence in liberation, remain foundational. Postcolonial criticism reexamines the Western canon, producing readings such as those of Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, which the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe attacked as dehumanizing Africa, or of Jane Eyre reread through the silenced Creole woman in the attic, a reading dramatized in Jean Rhys's novel Wide Sargasso Sea, which retells the story from her perspective. Equally important, it studies the rich literatures produced across Africa, the Caribbean, South Asia, and other formerly colonized regions, including the fraught question of language, whether a writer should use the colonizer's tongue, as many do to reach a global audience, or write in indigenous languages, a choice the Kenyan writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o made as an act of decolonization. Related fields, such as the study of diaspora, migration, and globalization, and the critique of how the very category of world literature is constructed, extend the inquiry. Critics have debated whether postcolonial theory, often written in dense academic prose within Western universities, adequately serves the peoples it studies, and whether its focus on discourse and identity neglects material inequality. Yet it decisively broadened literary study beyond the European tradition, insisting that literature and empire are entangled and that the reading of texts is inseparable from the global history of power, resistance, and cultural exchange.

sections.heading: Reader-Response, New Historicism, and Cultural Studies
sections.body: Several influential movements shifted the focus of criticism away from the isolated text toward, respectively, the reader, the historical archive, and the whole field of culture. Reader-response criticism, which gained prominence in the 1970s, challenged the New Critical dogma that meaning resides objectively in the text, arguing instead that a literary work exists only in the act of reading and that readers actively produce meaning rather than passively receiving it. Wolfgang Iser argued that texts are full of gaps and indeterminacies that the reader must fill, so that reading is a dynamic collaboration, while Stanley Fish provocatively contended that even the features we ascribe to a text are produced by the interpretive strategies we bring to it, and that meaning is determined by interpretive communities, the shared assumptions of groups of readers, rather than by the words alone. This approach usefully foregrounded the activity of reading but raised the worry that if readers make meaning freely, any interpretation is as good as any other, a relativism its defenders sought to limit by appeal to shared conventions. New Historicism, associated above all with Stephen Greenblatt and emerging in the 1980s in reaction to the ahistorical formalism of the New Criticism and the textual self-enclosure of deconstruction, returned criticism to history but in a new way. Rather than treating history as a stable background against which literature is set, New Historicists treat literary and non-literary texts as equally part of a single cultural fabric, reading a play alongside a medical treatise, a travel narrative, a legal record, or an account of an exorcism, and tracing the circulation of ideas, anxieties, and forms of power among them.
